prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "GOLDMAN SACHS GROUP INC" (ticker GS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "GS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc.
result.industry: Investment banking, trading and asset & wealth management
markets: Equities trading, prime brokerage and financing
Fixed income, currency and commodities (FICC) trading and financing
Ultra-high-net-worth wealth management and private banking
Transaction banking and consumer partnership cards (being wound down)

mission.statement: Goldman Sachs' mission is to advance sustainable economic growth and financial opportunity across the globe.
mission.source: Goldman Sachs 2019 Annual Report (Letter to Shareholders, 'Our Purpose and Core Values'); the current website states 'We aspire to be the world's most exceptional financial institution.'
mission.plain: Help the world's economy grow and give people and companies more chances to build wealth.

about.plain: Goldman Sachs is a big Wall Street bank that helps companies and governments raise money and buy or merge with other companies. It also buys and sells stocks, bonds and other investments for big investors like pension funds. And it looks after the savings of rich families and institutions, investing more than $4 trillion for them. It earns money from fees and from the small gaps between buying and selling prices.
about.customers: Large companies, governments, pension funds, hedge funds and very wealthy families.
about.everyday: When a famous company goes public on the stock market or two big brands merge, Goldman Sachs is often the bank that arranged it; it also issued the Apple Card until that program moves to Chase.

money.plain: Trading shares and lending to hedge funds (Equities)
Trading and financing bonds, currencies, commodities (FICC)

money.part: Managing money for institutions and the rich
money.plain: Fees for running funds and wealth accounts
Fees for mergers, IPOs and bond sales

money.part: Private-market investing and private banking loans
money.plain: Private credit, private equity gains, loans to wealthy clients

money.part: Consumer cards and transaction banking platform
money.plain: Apple Card and GM card programs being exited

result.summary: Goldman Sachs has a real but narrow moat built on its brand, its top-tier client relationships and its scale in deal advice and equities trading: it was No. 1 in global M&A in 2025, advising on $1.48 trillion of deals (about 32% of the market, LSEG). Its advantage is strongest in high-stakes advisory and institutional trading where reputation and balance sheet matter, but revenues are cyclical, talent is mobile, and it failed to build a consumer franchise (Marcus, Apple Card).

pricingPower.evidence: It led 2025 M&A fee rankings with about $4.6B of advisory fees versus $3.1B at JPMorgan and $3.0B at Morgan Stanley (LSEG), showing it commands premium mandates on the largest deals (38 of 68 deals over $10B), but underwriting and trading spreads are set competitively and fees fall with deal volumes, as in 2022-2023 when net revenues dropped to $47.4B and $46.3B from $59.3B in 2021.

moats.evidence: The Goldman name is the premier brand in investment banking; it ranked No. 1 in announced M&A and M&A fees in 2025 and its EMEA M&A share of 44.7% was the highest since 1999 (LSEG).
Prime brokerage, financing and ultra-wealthy private-bank clients are integrated into its systems and relationships, but corporate clients routinely split mandates across several banks.
Being the largest equities and M&A franchise brings the most order flow and deal information, which improves pricing and advice; equities net revenues were a record $16.5B in 2025.

A $2.1 trillion balance sheet and $4.1 trillion of assets under supervision (September 2026) let it fund large trades and spread technology costs, but JPMorgan has a larger, cheaper deposit-funded balance sheet.
Global investment banking is an oligopoly of a handful of bulge-bracket firms that can underwrite and trade at scale, which limits new entrants into top-tier mandates.
Its model is the incumbent one; it has not adopted a model rivals cannot copy, and its own attempt to disrupt consumer banking (Marcus, Apple Card) was abandoned.
Decades-old risk management culture (marking to market daily) and execution know-how on complex, cross-border deals are hard to replicate, though rivals have similar capabilities.
Its partner network and alumni are valuable, but bankers and traders can leave for rivals, hedge funds or private equity, so talent is not exclusive.

customers.evidence: It advised on 38 of the 68 deals of $10B or more in 2025 and its assets under supervision rose from $3.137 trillion at end-2024 to $4.097 trillion at September 30, 2026, showing institutional and wealthy clients keep returning; its consumer program (Apple Card) is moving to Chase after regulatory and service problems.

talent.evidence: Goldman remains one of the most sought-after employers for finance graduates, pays at the top of the industry, and the board granted $80M retention awards in restricted stock to CEO David Solomon and President John Waldron in January 2025, though senior partner departures have periodically drawn press attention.

product.evidence: It is No. 1 in global M&A advisory by deal value and fees in 2025 (LSEG) and a top-two equities trading house, while its wealth and alternatives platform passed $4 trillion of assets under supervision in 2026; its consumer products did not reach best-in-class.

threats: Cyclical collapse in deal and trading activity (net revenues fell from $59.3B in 2021 to $46.3B in 2023)
JPMorgan's larger deposit-funded balance sheet winning financing-led mandates and total IB fee share
Electronic market makers (Citadel Securities, Jane Street) taking share in equities and rates trading

Regulatory capital rules (Basel III endgame, stress capital buffer) and legal/reputational events (1MDB precedent)
CEO succession uncertainty as the board weighs handing the top job from David Solomon to John Waldron around 2027-2028
Talent poaching by hedge funds and private equity

ceo.name: David M. Solomon
ceo.background: Hamilton College BA in political science; leveraged-finance banker at Drexel Burnham and Bear Stearns before joining Goldman as a partner in 1999; co-head of investment banking, then president/COO

c1.evidence: Goldman leads investment banking (No. 1 in 2025 global M&A by deal value and fees, LSEG), but that is a mature, cyclical industry, not an emerging fast-growing one; net revenues grew at about 5.5% a year from $44.6B in 2020 to $58.3B in 2025.

c2.evidence: Clients choose Goldman for its brand, senior-banker access and execution on the biggest deals (38 of 68 deals over $10B in 2025), an advantage that has lasted over a century, though rivals such as JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley offer comparable services.

c3.evidence: Goldman Sachs is a household name and the default leader in M&A advice, but ordinary people mostly do not use its products, and its consumer push (Marcus, Apple Card) was retreated from, with Apple Card moving to Chase.

c4.evidence: Its stated mission 'to advance sustainable economic growth and financial opportunity across the globe' is not strongly emphasised day to day; management is focused on returns (ROE targets) rather than an inspiring purpose.

c6.evidence: “elite, powerful, wealthy, aggressive” - the impression is mixed: admired for prestige and competence, but often seen as greedy since the 2008 crisis (the 'vampire squid' image) and the 1MDB scandal.

c7.evidence: Global capital markets, M&A and wealth/alternatives are large and growing with the economy and the shift to private markets (Goldman's assets under supervision reached $4.1 trillion in September 2026), but there is no explosive secular tailwind like cloud or AI.

c8.evidence: It is expanding in private credit, alternatives and wealth management, but its biggest new-market attempt, consumer banking, failed and is being exited.

m1.evidence: Solomon set a clear strategy to grow durable asset and wealth management fees, but his earlier vision of a consumer bank was reversed in 2022-2026.

m2.evidence: Solomon is a professional manager (CEO since October 2018, not a founder) whose tenure has involved retention bonuses and publicised side interests such as DJing rather than founder-style ownership.

m4.evidence: Goldman emphasises clients first in its business principles, but Solomon's management style has been reported as demanding and the firm has had employee-morale controversies.

m5.evidence: Goldman has a strong, distinctive performance culture, but it is a culture of execution and client service rather than of inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Solomon is a leveraged-finance banker with a political science degree, not an engineer, though he has pushed AI tools across the firm.

m7.evidence: Solomon has led philanthropy such as One Million Black Women and 10,000 Small Businesses, but stewardship is mainly aimed at shareholder returns.

m7b.evidence: No commencement address by David Solomon at a top university such as Stanford, Harvard or MIT was found.

m8b.evidence: Solomon is known for a side career as 'DJ D-Sol', which made him memorable, but he is not a visionary personality in the Musk or Karp mould.

m9.evidence: Under Solomon net revenues rose from $44.6B in 2020 to $58.3B in 2025 and nine-month 2026 net revenues reached $56.2B, with annualised ROE of 20.7%, though the consumer bank write-downs were a costly mistake.

m10.evidence: Goldman is known for high pay and lavish compensation (operating expenses were $37.5B in 2025 on $58.3B of net revenues), not frugality.

c10.evidence: By helping companies and governments raise capital and manage risk it indirectly supports the global economy, but it does not directly improve the daily lives of large numbers of people.

p2.evidence: Executing trillion-dollar M&A and managing a $2.1 trillion balance sheet is hard and important to capital markets, but several rivals can do the same.

f1.evidence: Net revenues fell in 2022 ($47.4B from $59.3B) and 2023 ($46.3B) before rising to $53.5B in 2024 and $58.3B in 2025.

f2.evidence: Pre-tax margin rose from 28.0% in 2020 to 37.5% in 2025, but it swung from 45.6% in 2021 down to 23.2% in 2023; gross margin is not meaningful for a bank.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Goldman had $437.9B of unsecured borrowings against $187.3B of cash and total liabilities of $2.0 trillion against $122.7B of shareholders' equity (about 16x), normal for a broker-dealer bank but not low debt.

f4.evidence: Pre-tax earnings rose from $12.5B in 2020 to $21.9B in 2025 but were not rising every year (2022 $13.5B, 2023 $10.7B), and operating cash flow is volatile and was negative $25.8B in the first half of 2026.

v1.evidence: For the biggest M&A deals Goldman is widely seen as the best adviser (No. 1 by value and fees in 2025), but in trading, lending and wealth management it is one of several top peers.

v2.evidence: Goldman ranks among the most prestigious and sought-after finance employers, but it is also known for long hours and a demanding culture, and it is not usually near the top of broad best-workplace rankings.

c5.evidence: If Goldman disappeared, large companies, governments and institutional investors would miss a top adviser and market maker, but rivals could absorb its business and ordinary consumers would barely notice.
